cards.explanation: The answer is under a tent. David, Israel's king, tells Nathan, a prophet, "Here I am, living in a house of cedar, while the ark of the covenant of the LORD is under a tent." He's comparing his nice palace to the ark's tent. I think it's weighing on him.

The answer is True. Nathan the prophet answers King David with, "Do all that is in your heart, for God is with you." That's a quick, friendly yes. Hang on to it, friends, because God has more to say that night (1 Chronicles 17:3).

The answer is that David is not the one to build it. God tells Nathan to say, "You are not the one to build Me a house in which to dwell." God calls David "My servant" in the same breath. Nathan had just told David, "Do all that is in your heart…" and that night the word of God came to him. A prophet has to be ready to update his answer.

The answer is False. God puts it as a question: "In all My journeys with all the Israelites, have I ever asked any of the leaders I appointed to shepherd My people, ‘Why haven’t you built Me a house of cedar?’" The question points to no. In all those journeys, He never asked any of them. Not one of them was ever asked.

The answer is flock. God says to David, "I took you from the pasture, from following the flock, to be the ruler over My people Israel." David's start was following the flock, and God points back to it as part of how far he's come. I think that's a gentle reminder of who put him where he is.

The answer is a great name. God says to David, "Now I will make for you a name like that of the greatest in the land." He has been with David wherever he has gone and has cut off all his enemies. So this is God doing the making, not David. A name like that doesn't come from a business card.

The answer is False. God promises His people a place of their own where they will be "…disturbed no more." Then He says, "No longer will the sons of wickedness oppress them as they did at the beginning…" So once they're planted, they won't be oppressed like that anymore. That's a promise worth sitting down for.

The answer is that the LORD will build a house for David. David wanted to build God a house, and God flips it around. He says, "Moreover, I declare to you that the LORD will build a house for you." I think David didn't see that coming. He wanted to build God a house, and God answered with a promise to build his.

The answer is a house for God. God says of David's son, "He will build a house for Me…" So the job David wanted does get done. It just goes to the son God raises up after David. God also says He will establish that son's throne forever.

The answer is forever. God says about David's son, "…I will establish his throne forever." He says it again a couple of verses later: "…his throne will be established forever." That's no short-term promise, friends.

The answer is His loving devotion. God says about David's son, "I will be his Father, and he will be My son. And I will never remove My loving devotion from him as I removed it from your predecessor." Never is a strong word, and I'm glad God picked it.

The answer is that David asks who he is, that God has brought him this far. After hearing God's promises, David goes in, sits before the LORD, and says, "Who am I, O LORD God, and what is my house, that You have brought me this far?" He starts with a humble question, not a request. I think he's amazed at how far God has brought him.

The answer is knows. David says to God, "What more can David say to You for honoring Your servant? For You know Your servant, O LORD." He's run out of words. I think it's the kind of moment where you realize you don't need to explain yourself to God.

The answer is God's own heart. David says, "For the sake of Your servant and according to Your own heart, You have accomplished this great thing and made known all these great promises." So David credits God's own heart. Not his own, and not his plans.

The answer is that God went out to redeem them as a people for Himself. David calls Israel "…the one nation on earth whom God went out to redeem as a people for Himself?" He adds that God made a name for Himself through great and awesome wonders and redeemed them from Egypt. I think David is stunned that God went out for them.

The answer is False. David says to God, "For You have made Your people Israel Your very own forever, and You, O LORD, have become their God." So it's forever, not a little while. A little while would be a short lease, and this is nothing like that.

The answer is, "Do as You have promised." David prays, "And now, O LORD, let the word You have spoken concerning Your servant and his house be established forever. Do as You have promised…" His request is for God to do what He said. He goes on to ask that God's name be established and magnified forever, and that the house of David be established before Him.

The answer is that He is God over Israel. David wants it said, "The LORD of Hosts, the God of Israel, is God over Israel." That's the name he wants magnified forever. I think David cares more about God's name than his own.

The answer is courage. David says to God, "For You, my God, have revealed to Your servant that You will build a house for him. Therefore Your servant has found the courage to pray before You." The promise is what gave him courage. I bet it felt like a big door opening.

The answer is True. David closes his prayer with, "So now You have been pleased to bless the house of Your servant, that it may continue forever before You. For You, O LORD, have blessed it, and it will be blessed forever." He ends where God's promise left off. Forever is the last word of his prayer.
